strengths: Principled problem formulation: The paper tackles the challenging problem of achieving auto-calibration in probabilistic regression, directly addressing the well-known failure modes of weak marginal calibration (PIT) without resorting to restrictive parametric error assumptions (such as the Gaussian assumptions in Song et al., 2019).

Sound theoretical grounding: The calibration-sharpness decomposition based on generalized conditional mutual information (Lemma 4.1) and its formal unification with the grouping loss of Kull & Flach (2015) and Gneiting's paradigm (Proposition B.1) provide valuable theoretical insights into the score mechanics under auto-calibration.

Algorithmic contribution (EDK): Leveraging the Energy Distance Kernel (EDK) for continuous 1D target distributions enables an $O(m \log m)$ distance computation between empirical sample distributions of size $m$, overcoming the standard quadratic complexity $O(m^2)$ associated with kernel mean embeddings.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: The method is rigorously evaluated across four distinct probabilistic architectures (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF) on 11 datasets, evaluating both calibration hypothesis tests (SKCE and PIT) and scoring rules (CRPS), alongside extensive appendices covering conformal prediction, runtime ablations, and distribution regression comparisons.
weaknesses: Degradation of predictive density to discrete point-masses: The pre-image formulation approximates the recalibrated distribution by projecting the CKME weight vector onto the probability simplex $\Delta_{n_{\text{cal}}}$, resulting in an empirical distribution supported solely on the calibration target points $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cal}}}$. While acknowledged in Section 7, this completely discards any continuous density structure output by models like MDNs or GDNs.

Potential evaluation bias in SKCE testing: The hypothesis test of auto-calibration (Widmann et al., 2021) is implemented using the exact same Energy Distance Kernel (EDK) used in the proposed recalibration framework. While EDK is characteristic, utilizing the same kernel metric for both estimation and hypothesis testing creates a potential inductive bias that naturally favors CKME over baselines in SKCE acceptance rates.

CRPS performance penalty on small sample sizes: On datasets with smaller sample sizes (such as Yacht and Housing), CKME recalibration exhibits notable degradation in CRPS relative to the base model (e.g., relative CRPS reaching 1.276 on GDN, 1.326 on MDN, and 1.614 on BNN for Yacht), indicating that kernel estimation error can harm overall sharpness when calibration data is limited.

Scalability constraints of kernel inversion: The approach requires solving an $n_{\text{cal}} \times n_{\text{cal}}$ linear system with $O(n_{\text{cal}}^3)$ training complexity and $O(n_{\text{cal}})$ evaluation cost per test query. Scaling to larger datasets without approximations (e.g., Nyström, inducing points) remains an open challenge.

Presentation incomplete placeholders: The submission contains several empty URL placeholders for experiment code (e.g., Section 6, Appendix D.2, and Appendix F.2 end abruptly with 'publicly available at' or 'found at .').

strengths: Principled approach to auto-calibration: The paper addresses a well-known limitation of Probability Integral Transform (PIT) calibration (that marginal PIT uniformity permits severe local miscalibration via error cancellation) by formulating post-hoc recalibration as learning the auto-calibration map $Q \mapsto P_{Y|Q}$ nonparametrically via Conditional Kernel Mean Embeddings (CKME).

Insightful theoretical framing: The decomposition in Lemma 4.1 and Section 4 elegantly connects proper scoring rules, generalized conditional mutual information $I(Y; X|Q)$, and Kull & Flach's grouping loss, providing a clear information-theoretic perspective on the trade-off between calibration and sharpness.

Computational scalability via Energy Distance Kernel: The use of the Energy Distance Kernel (EDK) reduces the pairwise distribution kernel evaluation complexity for $m$-sample 1D empirical distributions to $O(m \log m)$ (compared to the standard $O(m^2)$), making distribution-space kernel regression practically viable.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across four distinct probabilistic regression models (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF) over ten UCI benchmarks and synthetic data, assessing both strong calibration (SKCE hypothesis testing), PIT goodness-of-fit, and predictive score (CRPS).
weaknesses: Potential evaluation bias with SKCE: The hypothesis testing for auto-calibration uses the SKCE test with the Energy Distance Kernel—the very same kernel family used to construct the CKME recalibration model. Testing with alternative distribution kernels (e.g., Gaussian MMD or Sinkhorn-based metrics) would help rule out favorable inductive alignment between the estimator and test statistic.

Heuristic simplification of the distributional pre-image: Transitioning from the exact pre-image objective in Eq. (39) ($(\theta - \beta)^T L (\theta - \beta)$) to the Euclidean projection in Eq. (40) ($(\theta - \beta)^T I_n (\theta - \beta)$) discards the target kernel geometry $L$. While computationally advantageous ($O(n)$ projection), the paper does not theoretically or empirically quantify the approximation error introduced by this substitution.

Support restriction and degradation on small sample sizes: Because the recalibrated distribution $\tilde{Q}^*$ is an empirical distribution supported solely on the calibration targets $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^{n_{cal}}$, the model loses continuous density modeling capabilities and cannot predict outside the convex hull of calibration targets. On small datasets (e.g., Yacht, Housing, Energy in Table 1), CKME leads to noticeable degradations in relative CRPS (e.g., up to 1.614 for BNN on Yacht), where simply training on $D_{train} \cup D_{cal}$ is much more competitive.
Incomplete repository links: In Section 6 (page 8) and Appendix D/F (page 17), URLs for the code repository are left blank (e.g., 'Our experiment code is publicly available at').

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in probabilistic regression: moving beyond marginal PIT uniformity to enforce auto-calibration without rigid parametric assumptions.

Provides a clean and intuitive theoretical framing in Section 4 and Appendix B, unifying the decomposition of proper scoring rules into auto-calibration error, lack of sharpness via generalized conditional mutual information, and aleatoric uncertainty.
Exploits the 1D Energy Distance Kernel (EDK) to reduce distribution kernel evaluation complexity from quadratic to $O(m \log m)$ for empirical distributions of size $m$.

Presents extensive empirical comparisons across 11 datasets and 4 model architectures, explicitly reporting statistical hypothesis test results (SKCE and PIT) alongside CRPS scores and conformal prediction comparisons.
weaknesses: Predictive quality as measured by CRPS is frequently compromised: on small-to-moderate datasets (e.g., Yacht, Housing, Concrete), CKME noticeably degrades the CRPS relative to the uncalibrated base model (CRPS ratios up to 1.61 for BNN on Yacht). Furthermore, simply retraining the base model on the combined training and calibration sets (None(T+C)) consistently achieves equal or better CRPS than CKME across almost all benchmarks.

Auto-calibration hypothesis testing still fails on larger datasets: in Figure 1, for datasets with higher test sample sizes (such as Kin8nm, Power, and Protein where the SKCE test has substantial statistical power), the null hypothesis of auto-calibration is rejected in the vast majority of splits, indicating limited recalibration effectiveness in data-rich regimes.

The distributional pre-image estimation relies on an unanalyzed heuristic: the authors substitute the target Gram matrix $L$ in Eq. (39) with the identity matrix $I_n$ (Eq. (40)) to enable standard Euclidean projection onto the simplex. This ignores the metric geometry and smoothness of the target space without theoretical error guarantees.

The resulting recalibrated predictions are discrete distributions supported exclusively on the calibration set targets $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^{n_{cal}}$, discarding the continuous density structure output by models such as MDNs or BNNs.

There is potential metric alignment bias in the evaluation: the SKCE hypothesis test was executed using the exact same Energy Distance Kernel employed by the proposed CKME algorithm, which may favor the method relative to baselines.
